chapter.title: Hume and Kant: where knowledge comes from

cards.body: Drop your phone. Did you watch gravity pull it down, or did you see a phone, then a floor? Around 1740 a Scot named David Hume raised his hand at the long table and said the second thing is all anyone ever sees. **We never see one thing cause another; we see one thing, then another.** Forty years later a Prussian professor, Immanuel Kant, stood up to answer him.
cards.simpler: Drop your phone. Did you watch gravity pull it down? Or did you just see a phone, then a floor? Around 1740 a Scottish thinker named David Hume said the second thing is all anyone ever sees. **We never see one thing cause another; we see one thing, then another.** Forty years later a German professor, Immanuel Kant, stood up to answer him.

cards.prompt: You flick the kitchen light switch and the light comes on. You have done this maybe 3,000 times. Strictly, what have your eyes seen?

options.text: A switch forcing a light to come on.
A switch moving, then a light on. 3,000 times.

whyNot.a: That's the link your mind adds, not what your eyes report: no eye has ever seen a 'forcing'.
whyNot.c: That's the explanation you were taught, not something you saw: the wire is inside the wall.

cards.reteach: Hume's trick is to split what you saw from what you concluded. You saw two events close together, over and over. The word 'caused' is the glue you put between them, and glue is not visible.

cards.title: Hume: the link is a habit
cards.body:
David Hume liked billiards for his example. Ball one rolls, touches ball two, ball two moves. Watch as closely as you like: you see motion, contact, motion. You never see a *necessary connection*, the thing that supposedly makes the second ball move.

So where does 'caused' come from? From *habit*: after you have seen the pair enough times, the mind jumps ahead. See the first ball, expect the second. **Cause, for Hume, is a feeling of expectation, not something out in the world.**

And the habit has no proof behind it. Tomorrow could differ from today. We just bet it won't.
cards.simpler:
Hume used billiard balls. Ball one rolls, touches ball two, ball two moves. Look as hard as you like. You see moving, touching, moving. You never see the push itself, the thing that makes ball two go.

So where does 'caused' come from? From habit. After you have seen the pair enough times, your mind jumps ahead. See ball one, expect ball two. **Cause, for Hume, is a feeling of expectation, not something out in the world.**

And that habit has no proof behind it. Tomorrow could be different. We just bet it won't.

cards.title: The cat and the fridge
cards.body: Ana's cat bolts to the kitchen whenever the fridge door opens. Two years, maybe 1,500 door openings, and food came out most times. The cat has a firm theory: fridge door causes dinner. One evening Ana opens the fridge for a phone charger she left on the shelf. The cat sits, waits, and is appalled. **Hume's uncomfortable point is that you are the cat, with more data.** Your 'fire causes burns' is built the same way, just from more pairs.
cards.simpler: Ana's cat runs to the kitchen whenever the fridge opens. Two years, about 1,500 openings, and food came out most times. The cat has a firm theory: fridge door causes dinner. One evening Ana opens the fridge for a phone charger she left on the shelf. The cat sits, waits, and is shocked. **Hume's uncomfortable point is that you are the cat, with more data.** Your 'fire causes burns' is built the same way, just from more pairs.

cards.prompt: A doctor says: 'Every patient who took this pill got better, so the pill cures the illness.' What would Hume say?

options.text: You watched the pill cure them, so the link is as visible as the pill.
You saw pill, then better, many times. The word 'cures' is habit filling the gap.
Your senses fooled you. The patients did not really get better.

whyNot.a: That's the link your mind added, not something in the data: nobody has watched a 'curing', only a pill and then a recovery.
whyNot.c: That's doubting the senses, which Hume never did: he trusted what you saw and questioned only the glue between the sightings.

cards.reteach: Hume does not say the pill failed. He says the doctor saw two events in a row, repeated, and let habit write 'because' between them. Habit may be right, but it is not something anyone observed.

cards.title: Kant: the link is a rule you bring
cards.body:
Immanuel Kant read Hume in Königsberg and later wrote that Hume woke him from a 'dogmatic slumber'. His reply came in 1781. Yes, cause is not in the raw sense data. But Hume got the source wrong.

**You cannot have an experience at all unless your mind has already sorted it into before and after, here and there, cause and effect.** Those are not habits you pick up. They are the mind's own rules, in place before the first billiard ball.

Think of glasses you cannot take off. Everything you see is tinted by them. Kant's price: we know the world as it looks through the glasses, never as it is on its own.
cards.simpler:
Kant read Hume and later said Hume woke him from a 'dogmatic slumber'. His reply came in 1781. Yes, cause is not in the raw stuff your senses give you. But Hume got the source wrong.

**You cannot have an experience at all unless your mind has already sorted it into before and after, here and there, cause and effect.** Those are not habits you learn. They are rules built into the mind, there before the first billiard ball.

Think of glasses you cannot take off. Everything looks tinted. Kant's price: we know the world as seen through the glasses, never as it is on its own.

cards.body: Priya, at the table, nods at Hume and says: 'So nothing really causes anything. I can rest my hand on the stove.' She has turned 'we never see the link' into 'there is no link'. Hume said neither; he said the link is supplied by us, and he kept his hands off stoves. **Spot it when a summary of Hume drops the word 'see'.**
cards.simpler: Priya nods at Hume and says: 'So nothing really causes anything. I can rest my hand on the stove.' She has turned 'we never see the link' into 'there is no link'. Hume said neither. He said the link is supplied by us, and he kept his own hands off stoves. **Spot it when a summary of Hume drops the word 'see'.**

cards.prompt: A friend asks for the one-line difference between Hume and Kant on cause and effect. Which line is right?

options.text: Hume: cause is a habit learned from repeated pairs. Kant: cause is a rule the mind brings to every experience.
Hume: cause is a rule the mind brings. Kant: cause is a habit learned from repetition.
Both: cause sits inside objects and we watch it directly, like colour.

whyNot.b: That's the two names swapped: the habit man is the Scot, the rules man is the Prussian who replied to him.
whyNot.c: That's the view both of them attacked: neither thought a 'causing' is ever seen, only the events on either side.

cards.reteach: Both agree your eyes never see a cause. They split on where the link comes from. Hume: from outside, by repetition, as a habit. Kant: from inside, as a rule built into how any mind must experience anything.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Hume said we never see one thing cause another, only one thing and then another, and **habit writes 'because' between them**. Kant replied that the 'because' is not a habit but a rule the mind must use to have any experience at all.

Tomorrow: Kant swaps 'what can I know' for 'what should I do', and Mill objects.
cards.simpler:
Hume said we never see one thing cause another. We only see one thing, then another, and **habit writes 'because' between them**. Kant replied that the 'because' is not a habit. It is a rule the mind must use to have any experience at all.

Tomorrow: Kant swaps 'what can I know' for 'what should I do', and Mill objects.

cards.body: Tonight, catch one 'because' you say out loud. 'The bus was late because of the rain.' Ask: did I see the rain make it late, or did I see rain, then lateness? That is Hume in 10 seconds.
cards.simpler: Tonight, catch one 'because' you say out loud. 'The bus was late because of the rain.' Then ask yourself: did I see the rain make it late, or did I see rain, then lateness? That is Hume in 10 seconds.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain, using cause and effect, why Hume said we never see one thing cause another and how Kant answered.
